intro: Almost Too Serious (Fast zu ernst) is No. 10 of Kinderszenen, Op. 15. It is in G♯ minor, and the piano’s melody runs across the barlines and stops repeatedly under fermatas.

sections.label: A · Tied melody in G♯ minor
A′ · Tied melody again
sections.mNote: The left hand resumes its rolling accompaniment

sections.label: Coda · Ritardando to a held chord

cues.title: Tied melody in 2/8
cues.text: The piece is in G♯ minor and in 2/8, so each bar holds two quavers. The melody ties its notes across the bar lines while the left hand plays semiquavers underneath. Schumann writes ritardandos before the fermatas, and both return through the piece.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, pp. 14–15: 2/8, five sharps, tied melody, semiquaver accompaniment and recurring ritardandos with fermatas. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The opening pattern returns, with the melody tied across the barlines over a turning left-hand accompaniment. The phrases again stop on fermatas. Each new phrase begins quietly.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 14–15: recurrence of the opening tied melody and accompaniment, with fermatas at phrase endings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kempowski’s childhood memoir, 1995
cues.text: Walter Kempowski printed this piece in musical notation at the front of his childhood memoir, published in Berlin in 1995. The book was titled Weltschmerz. Kinderszenen fast zu ernst (world-weariness, childhood scenes almost too serious).
cues.evidence: Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 36: Kempowski’s autobiographical collection, Berlin 1995, with Schumann’s score as its opening. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: Return of the tied opening melody
transitions.from: A · Tied melody in G♯ minor
transitions.how: The opening pattern of the G♯-minor song returns. The right hand holds notes across the short barlines, and the left hand plays the same rolling semiquavers as before. The dynamic stays quiet, and the pauses at the ends of phrases are kept.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, pp. 14–15, returning opening phrases. The section boundary locates the broad return.

transitions.title: Ritardando to the final G♯-minor chord
transitions.to: Coda · Ritardando to a held chord
transitions.how: In the final phrase the tied melody is drawn out above the rolling bass. A ritardando runs through the last bars, and both hands move towards a held G♯-minor chord. Fermatas in both staves stop the melody and the low bass together.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 15, final system: ritardando, closing G♯-minor chord and fermatas in both staves.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son, composer of piano music depicting lovers, masks and arguments, and a music critic.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
